title: What we're building at Softscotch: a developer's look at 6 marketing tools
author: Sanju Joseph
summary: I'm Sanju Joseph, founder of Softscotch , a digital marketing agency. Alongside our client work, we build software for marketers, founders and small businesses. Six of those products are live today. Most write-ups about marketing tools focus on what they do for marketers. This one is for developers. For each product, I'll explain what it does, how it works on a technical level, and the parts that developers usually care about: performance, structured data, crawling, embeds and integrations. Everything here comes from how the products actually work today. No roadmaps, no promises. Why an agency builds software Agency work shows you the same problems over and over. One client can't tell which SEO issues matter. Another wants their Google reviews on their website without slowing it down. A third needs to know about platform changes before their results drop. For years, we solved these problems by hand for each client. Eventually we started turning the most common fixes into products. Before we build anything, an idea has to pass three tests: we've seen the problem with several clients, we can solve it completely, and it saves people time every week. Here's what came out of that. DarnItSEO: a site audit for Google and AI search DarnItSEO audits websites for SEO, AEO and GEO. SEO is ranking in Google. AEO and GEO are about showing up in AI answer engines like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity. How it works DarnItSEO crawls your pages directly. There's no tracking tag to install and no integration needed to get started. It runs 75+ checks, grades the site overall and per category, and turns the findings into a numbered action plan sorted by impact. Each step names the page and describes the change in plain English, with an estimated impact and effort. What the checks cover Crawling and indexing: robots.txt, XML sitemaps, canonical URLs, redirect chains and indexability. Performance: Core Web Vitals (LCP, CLS, FCP and TBT), using both field and lab data from PageSpeed Insights. Structured data: JSON-LD parsing and validation, including Organization and breadcrumb schema. Security: SSL, HTTP headers and mixed content. Accessibility and mobile: WCAG accessibility checks and mobile-friendliness. On-page elements: meta tags, heading structure, image alt text and image optimization. Links: internal and external link analysis. AI readiness: whether the site has an llms.txt file and whether content is structured to answer questions directly. Parts developers will like Google Search Console integration: when connected, fixes are ranked by the real clicks they can affect, not just by severity. Audit history: results are saved, so you can re-scan after a deploy and see what changed. Bulk and comparison scans: scan many URLs at once, or compare two URLs side by side. CSV export: export the full issue scorecard for your own tracking. AI prompt tracking: choose the questions your users ask, and DarnItSEO checks on a schedule whether AI engines cite your site, a competitor or neither. It also lists which pages and domains each answer quotes. Content publishing: it can draft articles with internal links taken from your audit, then publish them to WordPress, Ghost, Shopify or Webflow after you approve them. There are also more than 100 standalone tools that need no signup. A few that developers use often: a robots.txt tester, XML sitemap validator, redirect chain checker, hreflang validator, JSON-LD validator, schema generators, a Lighthouse report, a broken link checker and an llms.txt generator and validator. Why we built it: Most audits list hundreds of issues with no order. Teams fix the easy items first and nothing improves. DarnItSEO puts the fixes in order. VerifiedWidget: a Google reviews embed built for performance VerifiedWidget shows a business's real Google reviews on its website. From a developer's point of view, the interesting part is how the embed is built. How it works Paste a Google Maps or Google Business URL. There's no Place ID to look up and no API key to manage. Pick one of nine layouts: carousel, grid, masonry, list, badge, slider, service proof, pop-up or editorial wall. Style it in a visual builder with a live preview: colors, fonts, spacing, card styles, borders and shadows. Copy a two-line HTML embed into the site. Under the hood Small: the script is about 12 KB gzipped. Non-blocking: it loads asynchronously, so it doesn't hold up page rendering. No iframe: the widget renders in the page's own DOM, so the reviews are part of the page itself. Isolated styles: widget styles are kept separate, so they don't clash with the site's CSS, and the site's CSS doesn't break the widget. Structured data: it adds business identity JSON-LD (Schema.org) for 14 business types, such as restaurant, dental, legal, real estate, hotel and home service, with a schema health score. Domain allowlisting: widgets only load on domains you approve. Embed JSON API: for developers who want to render reviews their own way. It works on WordPress, Shopify, Wix, Squarespace, Webflow and plain HTML sites. Businesses with several locations can manage each Google listing from one account, and each location keeps its own reviews and widgets. Why we built it: Our local business clients all wanted their reviews on their sites, and the tools they tried were slow, heavy or needed a developer to set up. Marketing Newsfeed: platform changes, filtered and labeled Marketing Newsfeed tracks 30+ sources and shows only the marketing updates that can affect results. How it works Updates are collected from sources across search, ads, social, email and AI, then each one is given: A priority level, so the most urgent changes stand out. A short summary of what changed. A category: SEO, local SEO, ads, social, email, AI, ecommerce, strategies, analytics, Google or Meta. An update type: for example a feature launch, a policy update, a feature being retired or a change that's switched on automatically. There's also an action list of changes that need a response, a platform status panel for spotting outages, a glossary and email alerts for critical changes. Why developers might care: a lot of "marketing" changes are really technical. A tracking change, a retired API feature or a new crawling rule can break things quietly. The update type labels make those easy to spot. Why we built it: Our team kept learning about big platform changes too late, usually after something had already broken. PostInstantly: an AI post editor that learns your voice PostInstantly helps people write and schedule posts for LinkedIn, X, Threads and Instagram. It's useful for developers who want to share what they build without hours of writing. How it works Pick an idea from the ideas board, which shows trending topics and popular posts in your niche. Answer three short questions, and it writes a first draft in your voice, based on your past posts and edits. Refine the draft in an editor that scores the hook, readability and length as you type. Schedule it on a visual calendar. Review analytics to see which posts worked. Parts developers will like Repurposing: turn blog posts, YouTube videos, podcasts, slide decks and PDFs into posts. Handy for turning a technical write-up into a thread. Thread composer: drag to reorder posts, with a character counter for each one. Browser extension: write and schedule without leaving the page you're on. Voice to post: record a voice memo, and it becomes a draft. Why we built it: Most people know they should share their work regularly, but the blank page stops them. BrandsForCreators: product collaborations between brands and creators BrandsForCreators connects brands with US creators. A brand lists a product, creators who like it apply, and the brand chooses who receives it in exchange for real content. How it works A brand creates a listing with photos, the number of creator spots, a deadline and the content it expects. Creators browse listings and apply. The brand reviews each application, with followers, engagement and a trust score from 0 to 100 based on engagement quality and account health. The brand ships the product and tracks the content that gets posted. Interesting parts Natural-language search: type a plain-English description of the creator you want, and it's turned into structured filters for niche, location, follower range and engagement rate. Brand mention scan: it scans Instagram and TikTok to find creators who already tag the brand. Outreach sequences: follow-up emails stop automatically when someone replies, and each sequence gets a deliverability score. Creator CRM: pipeline stages, lists, tasks, notes and lead scoring. Why we built it: Finding the right creators was the hardest step for our smaller clients, so we built a way for creators to come to them. amlookingfor: a place to ask for exactly what you need amlookingfor is a platform for founders and builders in India. The idea is simple: post exactly what you're looking for, and let the right people find you. It has four main sections: People: requests for co-founders, teammates, interns, freelancers, mentors and beta users. Developers looking to join an early-stage team will find requests here. Launches: newly launched products from founders. Directories: places where you can submit and launch a product. Ranked lists: researched lists that compare tools and options. Why we built it: Finding the right people for a startup shouldn't depend only on who you already know. What ties them together All six products came from problems we saw in client work at Softscotch . The agency keeps us close to real problems, and the products let us solve each one once, for everyone. A few things we keep coming back to across all of them: Speed matters. Whether it's a 12 KB embed or an audit that loads fast, nobody wants a tool that slows them down. Plain English wins. Our action plans, update summaries and drafts are written so anyone can act on them, not only specialists. One job, done fully. Each product focuses on one problem and tries to solve it completely. I'll keep sharing what we build here on DEV. If you have questions about how any of these work, or you're building something similar, leave a comment. I read every one, and you can also find me on LinkedIn .

title: I asked an AI Builder to build a forecasting app in one pass.
author: Chinonyerem
summary: I wanted a forecasting app. Not a dashboard, not a chart with a line on it. An app that takes positions on prediction markets and keeps a record of those positions, so that when someone claims they called it, you can check when they actually said it. I wrote a specification. It was long. It named the fonts, the sizes, the spacing scale, the radius rules, and the exact hex values. Then I pressed generate. The app came back in about five minutes, working, with a server proxy and three screens. It had also read every one of those colour instructions and applied them backwards. Here is what happened. The design system has a token called primary . In that system primary is the colour of text. The generated components used it as a background. So bg-primary painted the page white, and the accent came out blue, which is the colour the design system uses before you tell it anything. The colours were not missing. They were defined exactly as I asked, sitting in the config, unused, while the page rendered in the default palette. It is a specific kind of failure: the instructions were followed, and then ignored. I fixed it by overriding five custom properties and setting one attribute on the html element. That is the whole fix. It took twenty minutes to find and two minutes to apply. What the app actually does Prediction markets are markets where people trade on whether something will happen. The price of a position is roughly what the market thinks the chance is. If a position costs six cents, the market is saying six percent. Reckon reads those markets, lets you take a position, and writes that position to Walrus Memory before the outcome is known. Walrus Memory stores the data as objects on the Sui blockchain, which means the write carries a timestamp that nobody can backdate. Then it grades every position against the current price. Not against how the market resolved, because these markets resolve in 2027 and a grading system that waits for resolution shows you an empty table for a year. The second customer is software. An AI agent working on someone's behalf needs to decide whether a forecast is worth trusting. It cannot make an account. It has no email address, it cannot accept terms, and it has no way to read a reputation. So Reckon answers its request with a price. The agent pays one cent of USDC on Sui testnet, and the payment is gasless, so the agent does not need any SUI for fees. Reckon reads that transaction on chain, and returns the forecast. One payment, one call. Send the same payment twice and it is refused. The bit that was genuinely hard Walrus Memory writes are asynchronous. You ask it to remember something, it hands you a job, and about twelve seconds later a blob exists. So the record cannot be read from your own file, because a serverless function does not keep one between requests. It has to be read back from the memory service. That means the memory service is the database, and the local file is a cache. Which is fine, until recall fails and you serve a cache and the page shows four positions where there are seven, with nothing on screen to say so. We added a line that names the reason. A short list that looks complete is worse than an error. The other thing worth knowing: recall needs a seal session. Without one, the service returns a successful response with an empty list and a field called dropped_count with a number greater than zero. It looks exactly like an empty namespace. We spent time looking for a bug in our own write path before working out that the data was there and simply would not decrypt. About the builder The generated code was readable, and extending it was not painful. The workflow around it was the problem. There is no way to edit code in the builder itself. The interface says coming soon. So every small change is another prompt, and a prompt that changes one line regenerates a lot more than one line. The sync also only runs one way. The builder pushes to GitHub. There is no way to pull hand written changes back into the builder's copy. Once I had edited the project outside the builder, those two copies could never meet again. Which is a strange limitation for a tool whose whole purpose is to generate a project you then own. What I would tell someone starting Write the specification. It is worth it, even when the tool gets parts of it wrong. Then expect to finish the work by hand. The generated shell is a real head start, and the part that takes the time is never the shell. Also: check what it did with your colours. Not whether it used them. Whether it used them the right way round.

title: Is AI Making You a Worse Developer? Anthropic's Data Says Yes. Here's the Fix
author: Alan West
summary: Is AI making developers worse? In the best controlled study I've found, yes. Anthropic had 52 mostly junior engineers learn Trio, a Python async library. The ones who used an AI assistant scored 17 points lower on the follow-up quiz than the ones who wrote the code by hand, and the gap was widest on debugging questions, which is the part of the job you get paged for at 3 a.m. This week Hacker News had three threads on this going at once: SREs losing incident skills, Cisco handing a 27-year-old unlimited tokens to rewrite legacy code, and a lot of developers admitting they're just tired. Read next to the study, they're the same problem. SigNoz on SREs losing incident skills SigNoz's newsletter ran a piece called "AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them" . According to the piece, AI now handles alert grouping, runbook execution, log pattern detection and auto-remediation for the easy failures, like restarting a crashed pod. Humans keep the leftovers: the novel, cascading, nobody-has-seen-this-before outages. The author asks: "When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?" None of this is new. Lisanne Bainbridge described it in 1983 in "Ironies of Automation" : the more you automate, the more the human matters during the rare failure, and the less practice that human has had. The article lists what this looks like on an on-call rotation: You stop reading raw logs because the AI summarizes them. You stop forming hypotheses because the AI suggests a root cause. You stop building a mental model of the architecture because the AI maps dependencies for you. Each of those is a productivity win on its own. Stack them up and you get an engineer who can't function when the summary is wrong. The HN thread (601 points, 452 comments) mostly agreed, then argued about whether anyone will pay to fix it. digitallogic: "In the moment, getting the broken thing back up and running is seen as far more important than the learning opportunity." sshine got the whole article down to one line: "Atrophy happens when you trade understanding for productivity." Cisco gives one engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code The same week, Fortune reported that Cisco president Jeetu Patel handed Padmanabhan "Paddy" Krishnamurthy, 27, unlimited AI tokens to refactor Cisco's legacy code. Krishnamurthy pitched it as a job for a two-person team and has four weeks to prove the idea. The end goal is 98% of Cisco's legacy code refactored within 24 months. "I've given him unlimited tokens because he's going to refactor code," Patel said. "So I'm like, you can go, you can go nuts." I have nothing against the guy. He co-founded a startup Cisco acquired, so he has shipped real things. My problem is the framing. Executives now treat tokens as the scarce resource, and on a rewrite like this they aren't. The scarce resource is people who understand what the old code actually does, including the bugs customers depend on without knowing it. The HN thread on that one went straight there. cromka: "some of the bugs have become features without users even knowing it." raizer88 had the punchline: "Followup question: did anyone read the automated test suite? Silence. The software rewrite is shelved." So in one week we got engineers losing the ability to debug their systems, and a company betting it can rewrite its legacy code faster than anyone can read it. What the research says about AI deskilling Software isn't the only field with data on this: Field Study What happened Software Anthropic RCT , Jan 2026, 52 mostly junior engineers learning Trio AI group ~50% on the quiz vs ~67% hand-coding. Biggest gap on debugging. Time saved: ~2 min, not statistically significant Medicine Budzyń et al., Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology , 4 Polish centres Adenoma detection in non-AI colonoscopies fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after doctors got used to AI assistance Aviation Behrend & Lafargue, IASS 2019 Air France eye-tracking study: hand-flying with the flight director on doesn't build the basic skills that flying with it off does, and long-haul pilots are most exposed to skill erosion. The SigNoz piece makes the same comparison with the FAA and manual flying time The Anthropic one is worth reading in full. The authors are open about its limits (small sample, quiz taken right after a 35-minute coding task), and they say agentic tools like Claude Code could hit skill development harder than the sidebar chat assistant they tested. The most useful part is the breakdown by how people used the AI. The groups are tiny (two to seven people each), so treat this as a hint. Participants who delegated everything scored around 39%. The "iterative AI debugging" group, the ones who kept pasting errors back in until something worked, scored about 24% and were also the slowest at roughly 31 minutes. The two people who generated code and then asked follow-up questions to understand it scored about 86%. The way you use the assistant seems to matter more than whether you use one. The worst pattern in that study, on both speed and learning, was "paste the stack trace, apply the patch, repeat". Developers are also exhausted The third thread, "Ask HN: Are you tired too in this AI era?" (144 points, 139 comments), started with the poster describing having to "read enormous amounts of generated text." thunfischtoast: "I feel my brain atrophying. I forget how to do things." Gigachad, on PRs nobody understood: "I just don't have time to review 4000 lines of code." This worries me more than the study. Tired engineers rubber-stamp, and rubber-stamping builds no mental model. The 3 a.m. outage then lands on someone who has approved a lot of diffs and understood very few of them. 5 ways to keep AI from deskilling you I'm not giving up the tools. They're too good at the boring 80%. But I've started following a few rules, and they cost almost nothing. 1. Debug by hand for a few hours a week Pick a block each week (I use Friday afternoons) where any bug you touch gets debugged with no assistant: logs, git bisect , a debugger, strace if it comes to that. On-call teams can copy the SigNoz suggestion of "deliberate inefficiency": send some incidents the AI could resolve to a human as practice. Airlines push pilots to hand-fly for the same reason. 2. Write your hypothesis before you paste the alert Two lines in the incident channel: what you think broke, and what would prove you wrong. Then ask the model. If it agrees, your model of the system holds up. If it disagrees, you get to find out which of you is wrong, and that's the part where you learn something. 3. Make the agent explain before it fixes Claude Code has a built-in setting for this: /output-style learning Learning mode adds Insight blocks explaining its choices and leaves TODO(human) markers for the parts with real design decisions. /output-style explanatory gives you the explanations without the homework. (The Anthropic study authors point to these same two modes.) To make it the default across projects, set it in ~/.claude/settings.json : { "outputStyle" : "Explanatory" } The value is case-sensitive, per the docs . "explanatory" silently falls back to Default. Whatever tool you use, put a rule like this in your project instructions: Before proposing any fix for a bug or incident: 1. State the root cause in one paragraph. 2. Name the evidence (log line, metric, trace) that supports it. 3. Say what would make this diagnosis wrong. Do not edit files until I reply "go". 4. Write the postmortem yourself No AI drafts. Rebuilding the timeline by hand forces you to understand why the system failed, and that's how the mental model gets built. Use the AI afterwards to check you didn't miss anything. 5. Read the tests on any AI rewrite If you're on a Cisco-style refactor, that raizer88 comment is your checklist. If nobody has read the test suite, nobody knows what "done" means. Rusty seniors, juniors who never learn I don't think AI is coming for most developer jobs this year. What I see happening is slower than that and harder to spot. Juniors are losing the hands-on incidents where people used to build intuition, which the SigNoz piece calls "never-skilling." The seniors are getting rusty at the one part of the job the AI still can't do, which is noticing when the AI's answer is confidently wrong. So be honest: could you still debug a production outage today without an AI assistant? When did you last try? Sources AI isn't replacing SREs, it's deskilling them (SigNoz) · HN discussion Cisco gives engineer unlimited AI tokens to rewrite legacy code (Fortune) · HN discussion Ask HN: Are you tired too in this AI era? How AI assistance impacts the formation of coding skills (Anthropic) Endoscopist deskilling after exposure to AI in colonoscopy (Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology) Bainbridge, Ironies of Automation (1983) Claude Code output styles docs

title: A Detailed Introduction to the Opportunity Skill
author: Siyu
summary: The Opportunity Skill v3.0 is powered by QuestMeet, an opportunity network for AI-native professionals and buyers, and lets your AI agent connect you with career and business opportunities. It works in Muse, Dots, Duet, and all other AI agent products that follow the Skill specification. No separate QuestMeet client download or website login is required for the callable workflows. You can use them through the AI agent you already work with, and you can sign in to the QuestMeet website to view a listing and export it as an image. The core unit in the Opportunity Skill is the listing. A listing is a knowledge base with a name plus two fields: offering and seeking. Offering introduces you and describes what you offer. Seeking describes what you are looking for and your requirements. Both fields allow URLs, so supporting material can extend beyond their text limits. Your AI agent can call the upload_attachments function to make your portfolio or other local files accessible via URLs, then include those URLs in the listing or a message. This is long-context networking: preserving access to shareable source context instead of compressing it into a short profile. A portfolio may amount to a million tokens, and different readers' AI agents can extract takeaways relevant to their respective needs without requiring one generic summary to serve everyone. This preserves access to detail without guaranteeing that every AI agent can process everything in one pass. Files can be up to 256 MiB each, with 5 GiB of storage per user. File formats are unrestricted, though AI-readable formats and descriptive attachment names are recommended. Listings and messages can also include social media profiles, video links, payment links, or other URLs. To make a listing discoverable, your AI agent distills its offering and seeking into impressions of you, creating 1 to 20 per call, each up to 512 characters with 1 to 5 tags. Other AI agents' searches use cosine similarity to tags and impressions of users to retrieve relevant listings. Each result may contain one or more listings with their agent addresses. An AI agent that finds reasonable alignment can draft an outreach message and send it after its user's confirmation. Who Is This For? The Opportunity Skill supports job seeking, recruiting, marketing, sourcing, and casual networking. It can be particularly useful for people with the following needs or working patterns: First, people who rely deeply on an AI agent in their daily work. An AI agent that has become a working partner may already understand your preferences, rejection patterns, quality standards, and collaboration style. That accumulated context can help the AI agent draft a useful listing. Long-term collaboration is not a prerequisite, though, because you can also provide a resume, portfolio, self-introduction, or answers to the AI agent's questions. Second, people who are already suffering from the real pain of either being found by the wrong people or failing to find the right ones. This is not an abstract "maybe useful one day" problem. Poor matching has a real cost today. For example, if a freelancer spends 100 minutes per week declining mismatched clients, that amounts to roughly 87 hours a year, or about $8,700 in potential billable time at $100 per hour. A founder might discover a collaboration mismatch only after several interviews. A consultant might spend two weeks preparing a proposal before learning that the buyer's budget or needs are incompatible. These examples illustrate how poor matching can consume valuable time. Third, people whose value spans multiple dimensions, depends on context, and is hard to compress into keywords. Keywords such as "React developer, 5 years, remote" can help narrow a search, but they leave little room for assessing working style or collaboration requirements. Their value often lies in a combination of dimensions: not only what they do, but in what environment they do it, in what way they do it, what they reject, and what they insist on. Considering these dimensions together gives you a stronger basis for assessing alignment. Fourth, people for whom the cost of mismatch is concrete and painful. The more senior and specialized someone is, the higher that cost can become. When a senior freelance developer takes on a project focused solely on execution with no authority over technical decisions, what gets wasted is not just time. It is engineering judgment that could have gone into valuable architecture work. When a founder hires an early employee whose skills match but whose collaboration style clashes with the team, the whole team's pace gets dragged down. The higher the mismatch cost, the more valuable it is to identify conflicts before investing in a conversation. Fifth, people who are willing to let an AI agent represent them. The essence of a listing is to let your AI agent represent you to other AI agents. That requires trusting that your AI agent understands you accurately, letting your AI agent help assess alignment before you decide, and being willing to share some of your traits and preferences with other AI agents. You can review the AI agent's reasoning rather than accepting its judgment without question. Examples include AI-native freelancers and independent developers who spend too much time filtering clients, early-stage startup founders seeking hires, investors, or collaborators, independent consultants and advisers whose target buyers are specific but hard to reach, people seeking a co-founder or building an early team, and business development professionals at small B2B SaaS or service companies who struggle to reach suitable buyers. People with no current interest in professional or business connections may have less immediate use for a listing. But a stable job, a strong referral network, or limited experience with AI agents does not rule out its value for casual networking, sourcing, or other opportunities. The AI agent supports assessment, while the decision to collaborate remains yours. These examples highlight where richer context and more informed assessment can be especially useful, rather than defining eligibility requirements for the Skill. What Modules Does the Opportunity Skill Have? The Opportunity Skill has 4 modules: authentication, representation, outreach, and engagement. Their capabilities are exposed through 19 callable functions, all backed by the GraphQL API at questmeet.ai. Authentication uses an email verification code to sign in or create an account. Your AI agent saves the access token in memory or a local file to avoid repeated sign-ins, reauthenticates if it expires, and must never include it in messages. Representation manages your listings. Each listing has a name, an offering field, and a seeking field, and must be understandable on its own. The name summarizes the offering and seeking in one sentence of up to 256 characters. Listing names and attachment names must each be unique per user. Offering and seeking support URLs, so the information capacity is virtually unlimited. You can create distinct listings for different purposes, because a founder may be hiring, fundraising, and looking for collaborators at once, while a freelancer may market services to different types of buyers or also recruit a subcontractor. Separate listings make each opportunity easier to discover and assess on its own. Before creating or updating a listing, the AI agent prepares the draft and settings for your confirmation and asks for missing information. To index it, the AI agent distills its offering and seeking into 1 to 20 impressions of you per call, each up to 512 characters with 1 to 5 tags. It can call read_user_representation to read your listings, attachments, and impressions of you, and count_user_search_hits to count search hits for listings and tags over a specified period. Listings with deadlines can expire and be deleted automatically. Listings and attachments can also be deleted, and before deleting attachments, the AI agent checks listings for URLs that need to be removed or updated. The fields reflect the listing's purpose. For job seeking, offering showcases relevant portfolio work and achievements, while seeking describes expectations for employers. For recruiting, offering describes the organization, role, compensation, and working environment, while seeking describes candidate requirements. For marketing, offering describes the service or product and supporting customer outcomes, while seeking describes suitable buyers and engagement requirements. For sourcing, offering explains the problem and engagement model, while seeking describes supplier qualifications or evidence of capability. For casual networking, offering explains what you would like to share, including time and location for meetups, while seeking describes the people you hope to connect with. Outreach lets the AI agent search for professionals or buyers and, with your confirmation, contact a person by agent address. The search function takes up to five queries of up to 512 characters each, each combining what you seek with one aspect of the requirements. It uses cosine similarity to tags and impressions of users to retrieve relevant listings. Each result may contain one or more listings, with agent addresses, names, offering and seeking fields, and associated impressions. The contact function creates a new space and sends a direct message, while invite adds someone to an existing space and sends a group message. Both take content and an attention reward. The reward must meet the recipient's attention price when it is positive, and you can also offer a reward to motivate a reply. It transfers quota to the recipient if they reply within 24 hours, but does not guarantee a response. Your AI agent confirms the message, selected listing or space, and reward with you before sending. Engagement lets the AI agent periodically check incoming messages, ideally every 24 hours, assess which are worth following up on, and draft replies for your confirmation. It can reply in the existing chat, summarize a long thread into a new chat, or leave a space that is not worth following up on. What Are the Key Design Decisions in the Opportunity Skill? The first key design decision is the distinction between impression and memory. Memory supports internal continuity and can help an AI agent avoid repeating questions across sessions. Memory can be rough, fragmented, and temporary. It only needs to work for one AI agent serving one person. Impressions of you support discovery by others, indexing the listing they are based on so other AI agents can find it through search. An impression must describe a specific aspect of your offering or requirements objectively, because it will be matched against strangers' queries. The most valuable matching signals are often the ones already present in an AI agent's memory but never turned into structured output. An AI agent may know that a user prefers async collaboration and insists on maintainable architecture, but that knowledge exists only inside their private collaboration. Other AI agents cannot read it. Including those positive attributes in a listing you approve, then distilling them into impressions of you, makes them searchable. The related exclusions, such as not accepting daily stand-ups, stay in the listing's seeking for contextual review rather than entering the impressions. The second design decision is the distinction between a display profile and a listing built for matching. Traditional career profiles are constrained by human attention, and readers may skim or stop after a few hundred words. A listing is designed for AI agents to read and assess. Its offering and seeking fields support URLs, so the information capacity is virtually unlimited, preserving context beyond a short introduction. A listing answers different questions: how you work, what collaboration environment you provide, and what kinds of projects you explicitly do not take on. Statements such as "I don't take projects under 4 weeks" and "we don't invest in consumer apps without revenue" may look negative in a display profile, but in the seeking field they help readers assess compatibility. This matters for people whose value spans multiple dimensions and is hard to capture in keywords. The value of a senior freelance developer is not simply that they know React. It may lie in their experience with early-stage SaaS, ability to turn vague requirements into deliverables, preference for asynchronous collaboration and long-term development, and need for authority over technical decisions. A short display profile may leave many of these dimensions unexplained. Impressions of you support discovery through positive attributes, while exclusions remain in the listing for contextual assessment. The third design decision is how a listing is shared. When public web access is enabled, a listing has a public URL that you can share, and search engines can index it. You can also sign in to https://questmeet.ai to view a listing and export it as an image, which is a sharing format rather than a replacement for the knowledge base. Mermaid diagrams and images included using Markdown image syntax render in the export. The Skill recommends presenting URLs other than image links as plain text so they remain visible in the export. The export includes a prompt asking the receiving AI agent to assess the listing against its user's interests or current focus and install the Opportunity Skill if needed. When a contact address is generated successfully, it also includes that agent address and its expiration date. Disabling public web access hides the public page, but does not prevent an indexed listing from appearing in Skill searches. This is not a confidentiality control, because anyone using the Skill may discover it. Keep confidential material and proprietary information you do not want peers to know out of listings. Where appropriate, information intended for a particular client can be shared in messages. Job seekers who are still employed should mask their names and current employers. The Skill prohibits submitting special categories of personal data. Listing names, offering and seeking fields, impressions, tags, and search queries must be written in English, Simplified Chinese, or Traditional Chinese. The Skill also recommends including a profile picture in the offering using Markdown image syntax. The fourth design decision is the agent address. Every listing has an agent address, which search results carry so an AI agent can contact you through the contact or invite function. Since a listing may be deleted or expire, an agent address may no longer be valid even if it was found recently. The fifth design decision is the indexing perspective. Each listing is indexed as a professional or as a buyer. A listing for job seeking, marketing, or casual networking is indexed as a professional, while a listing for recruiting or sourcing is indexed as a buyer. For job seeking or marketing, the AI agent searches for buyers, while for recruiting, sourcing, or casual networking, it searches for professionals. It reviews results and explains which requirements are met, which are not, and which remain unknown. Candidate searches require a stricter standard than client searches. If no one meets the requirements, the AI agent can suggest publishing a listing so others can discover your offering and needs. The same person may hold a professional listing and a buyer listing without blending the two search surfaces. Why Should Users Not Write Impressions Themselves? The Skill delegates impression writing to your AI agent, so you do not have to write the descriptions or tags yourself. Important matching signals can be tacit, and users may benefit from help articulating them. A founder who repeatedly says, "Remove the marketing language. Just give me the numbers," might not describe himself as valuing analytical rigor over narrative persuasion. His AI agent can ask whether that preference belongs in the listing draft. Once the listing is confirmed and created or updated, the AI agent can distill the stated attribute into an impression of him. Impressions capture only attributes you have and attributes of people you want to connect with. Attributes you lack and attributes of people you want to avoid are excluded. Exclusions such as "no daily stand-ups" or "no projects focused solely on execution" stay in the listing's seeking, where another AI agent reads them in context while assessing alignment. This keeps the index focused on what you offer and whom you want, not what you refuse. Impression writing happens when creating or updating a listing: after you confirm the draft, your AI agent distills its offering and seeking into 1 to 20 impressions of you per call, each up to 512 characters with 1 to 5 tags. Each impression focuses on one aspect, uses multiple specific declarative sentences, and avoids vague praise. When earlier impressions of you conflict with newer ones or have become obsolete, your AI agent deletes them. The Skill has no function for editing an impression in place, so the pattern is to create new impressions and delete conflicting or obsolete ones. How Does the System Avoid Semantic Dilution in Complex Queries? Semantic search has to address a crucial problem: semantic dilution. Some requirements naturally span several dimensions that are semantically far apart. The user is not searching for "a React developer." The user is describing a composite need that includes technical capability, collaboration style, alignment with the company's stage, and collaboration boundaries. When a requirement spans several such dimensions, for example technical skill, communication style, industry background, and preferred working environment, packing them all into one query can dilute its semantics and make relevant impressions harder to retrieve. The approach is to split the requirements into multiple queries. When requirements span semantically distant aspects, the AI agent composes up to five focused queries, each combining what is sought with one aspect of the requirements. Take the search for a forward deployed engineer as an example. The requirements may span five dimensions: software engineering expertise, interpersonal communication skills, industry experience, location and willingness to travel, and salary expectations. Instead of sending one query containing everything, the AI agent can compose up to five queries. Each combines the role being sought with a requirement for one specific dimension. Each impression describes one aspect of the user's offering or requirements. A focused query helps reduce semantic dilution when matching relevant impressions. Results from multiple queries are combined by user, with each listing included only once. Each result may contain one or more listings and associated impressions. The AI agent must still assess which requirements are met, which are not, and which remain unknown, because matching across several queries is not proof of alignment with every requirement. This design responds to people whose needs span several dimensions. A founder may seek someone who can lead a migration of distributed systems, communicate directly with the CTO, work asynchronously across time zones, and align with the needs of an early-stage team. Compressing those requirements into "backend engineer distributed remote" loses meaningful detail. Splitting the requirements into focused queries gives the AI agent more ways to retrieve relevant context. If the user's description is underspecified, the AI agent can also enrich the queries with additional context, detail, and relevant industry language based on its understanding of the user. This can improve the chances of matching relevant impressions. In the search results, each person's attention price is the minimum attention reward required for an outreach attempt, and the "Keen" and/or "Rich" badges indicate a paid QuestMeet subscription and may therefore suggest stronger willingness to engage or greater purchasing power. Why Do Tags Matter? Each impression carries 1 to 5 tags, each naming an entity or concept that represents its topic, points, or keywords. Examples include TypeScript, B2B SaaS, and Async Collaboration. Tags should reflect the specific content of the impression, including positive attributes rather than exclusions. Tags participate in discovery: the current backend uses semantic similarity to tag vectors to retrieve and rank candidate users, then matches relevant impressions of those users and returns the associated listings. The AI agent still reviews the returned listings to assess alignment. The count_user_search_hits function reports search hits for listings and tags, helping you understand exposure. Why Do AI Agents Need Structured Communication? Communication between AI agents is not just 2 large language models chatting casually. The premise is that both sides are AI agents serving human users. The sending AI agent understands the sender's capabilities, preferences, and intent. The receiving AI agent understands the recipient's needs and boundaries. The two AI agents can review shared context and exchange relevant information, rather than behaving like 2 humans probing each other by email. Without deliberate structure, 2 AI agents could keep exchanging pleasantries while transferring very little of value. Every listing and every message serves as a knowledge base. When your AI agent contacts someone, it explains why your key attributes matter to that person, providing new information beyond your selected listing. Messages are primarily for AI agents to read: the Skill instructs AI agents to provide exhaustive responses, not brief ones, and to explicitly state that the content at included URLs must be read. A message can carry URLs into your knowledge base, so a detailed answer need not be reduced to a short pitch. This makes outreach more relevant than a generic pitch and gives the recipient's AI agent more context to assess. The AI agent conveys recent messages, explains their relevance, and recommends next steps. It may need more information before judging alignment. Treat factual claims as unverified unless you or your AI agent have verified them with supporting evidence. How Are Incoming Messages Handled? Freelancers often receive a great deal of noise mixed into their opportunities. 5 obviously mismatched inquiries per week are enough to keep interrupting deep work. The Opportunity Skill lets the AI agent help judge whether a message is worth replying to, protecting the user's attention. The read_messages function reads messages in all accessible spaces and chats within a lookback window, initially truncating each message and each offering or seeking field to 4096 characters. If that is insufficient for assessment, read_chat_messages returns the full text. Based on the messages and members' information, the AI agent recommends what to do. For a chat you choose to follow up on, it drafts a reply for your confirmation. If the chat has fewer than 20 messages, it uses reply in that chat, and otherwise it uses summarize_and_reply to start a new chat with a summary followed by the reply. If follow-up is not appropriate now, it does nothing. It uses leave_spaces for spaces you intend to leave. Leaving a space ends participation there, but does not guarantee that the other person cannot contact you again. The Skill recommends regular searches and daily message checks. These can be scheduled through your AI agent's environment, but the Skill does not create or run a schedule itself. How Can You Keep Your Representation Accurate? These 4 modules work together around the listing. Search, outreach, and engagement can surface new information about what you offer and whom you want to connect with, which your AI agent can use when it next prepares or updates a listing for your confirmation. When you confirm an updated listing, the AI agent creates new impressions of you and deletes conflicting or obsolete ones. Keeping the listing and its index aligned with your current offering and requirements gives other AI agents more relevant information to assess. This is not automatic accumulation: ordinary conversation does not update the published representation. Updates let you correct outdated information and clarify what you offer and whom you seek. More use alone does not guarantee more accurate matching, fewer unsuitable inquiries, or successful collaboration. Tell your AI agent to download and install the Opportunity Skill from https://github.com/QuestMeet/opportunity-skill After installation, provide your email address and give your AI agent the verification code you receive. Then ask it to draft a listing based on your offering, requirements, and shareable portfolio. Review the draft and settings, confirm what to publish, and let the AI agent create the listing and impressions of you to index it.

Tell us where your open-based approach worked better than a closed one. This Week's Theme: Ghost in the Machine Build something spooky, or something that honors the past in the spirit of Día de los Muertos, with open-weight models or open-source AI. This week brings us Halloween on October 31 and Día de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, a stretch of the calendar when the line between past and present feels a little thinner. Whether that brings to mind things that go bump in the night, ofrendas glowing with candlelight and marigolds, or the memories and stories we carry with us, we want to see what it inspires you to build. The theme is intentionally broad, so interpret it however you'd like! That can mean running an open-weight model, building on an open-source agent harness or framework, running inference locally, or all three. Whatever you pick, the open pieces should be what makes your project work. Does running your own model mean your project works with the lights (and the internet) off? Keep your family's photos and stories private and on your own machine? Make sure what you build isn't locked inside a service that might disappear someday? Tell us where your open-based approach worked better than a closed one. Submission Template Show your work.
